blocks.text: Sprinkle salt on sliced cucumber and within minutes water beads on the surface and the slices go limp. Soak a wilted ugu leaf in clean water and it becomes firm again. The same process explains both — water moving across cell membranes by osmosis.

blocks.markdown:
## Three ways substances cross a membrane

**Diffusion** is the net movement of particles of a gas or a dissolved substance from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration, down a concentration gradient. It is passive: it needs no energy from the cell, only the random movement the particles already have.

**Osmosis** is a special case of diffusion involving water. It is the movement of water molecules from a dilute solution (high water potential) to a concentrated solution (low water potential) through a partially permeable membrane. It is also passive.

**Active transport** is the movement of a substance *against* its concentration gradient, from low to high concentration, using energy from respiration and carrier proteins in the membrane. Because it needs ATP, it stops if the cell is deprived of oxygen or poisoned with cyanide.

blocks.title: Partially permeable membrane
blocks.text: A membrane that lets small molecules such as water pass through freely but restricts larger solute molecules such as sucrose. Visking tubing behaves this way, which is why it is used in classroom osmosis experiments.

blocks.caption: Comparing the three transport processes

blocks.markdown:
### What osmosis does to a cell

What happens depends on the surrounding solution and on whether the cell has a wall.

A **plant cell** placed in pure water or a dilute solution (hypotonic) gains water. The vacuole swells and pushes the cytoplasm against the wall. The wall resists, so pressure builds and the cell becomes firm, or **turgid**. Turgor is what holds a herbaceous plant upright.

The same plant cell placed in a concentrated solution (hypertonic) loses water. The vacuole shrinks, the cytoplasm and membrane pull away from the wall, and the cell is **plasmolysed**. A whole plant in that state is **flaccid** and has wilted. If the cell is returned to water soon enough it recovers — this is **deplasmolysis**.

An **animal cell** has no wall to resist the pressure. In pure water a red blood cell swells and bursts; this is **haemolysis**. In a concentrated solution it shrinks and its surface becomes wrinkled, or **crenated**. This is why fluid given to a patient by drip must be isotonic with blood.

blocks.title: Predicting the direction of water movement
blocks.prompt: A piece of Visking tubing is filled with 20% sugar solution, tied at both ends and placed in a beaker of 5% sugar solution. What happens to the mass of the tubing, and why?

steps.text: Identify which solution is more dilute. The beaker at 5% sugar has more water per unit volume, so it has the higher water potential.
Identify the membrane. Visking tubing is partially permeable: water molecules can cross it but sugar molecules are too large.
Apply the rule for osmosis: water moves from the dilute solution to the concentrated solution. So water moves from the beaker into the tubing.
Deduce the observable result. The tubing gains water, so its mass and volume increase and it becomes firm; the solution in the beaker becomes slightly more concentrated.
Note the endpoint. Net movement slows and stops once the two solutions reach the same concentration, though individual molecules keep moving both ways.

blocks.answer: The mass of the tubing increases, because water moves by osmosis from the more dilute 5% solution outside into the more concentrated 20% solution inside.

items: Root hair cells absorb water from the soil by osmosis, because soil water is more dilute than the cell sap.
Root hair cells absorb mineral salts by active transport, because the soil usually contains fewer ions than the cell already holds.
Oxygen passes from the alveolus into the blood, and carbon dioxide the other way, by diffusion.
Glucose and amino acids are reabsorbed from the kidney tubule back into the blood by active transport.
Digested food is absorbed from the ileum by both diffusion and active transport.

blocks.title: Do not say 'water concentration' loosely
blocks.text: Say that water moves from a dilute solution to a concentrated solution, or from high water potential to low water potential. Writing that water moves 'from high concentration to low concentration' without saying concentration of what is the commonest way marks are lost here.

blocks.title: Spotting active transport in a question
blocks.text: If a question says uptake stopped when the tissue was placed in nitrogen, cooled, or treated with a respiratory poison, the process involved is active transport, because only active transport depends on energy from respiration.

points: Diffusion moves particles down a concentration gradient and needs no energy.
Osmosis moves water through a partially permeable membrane from a dilute to a concentrated solution.
Active transport moves substances against the gradient using carrier proteins and energy from respiration.
A plant cell in water becomes turgid; in a concentrated solution it becomes plasmolysed and the plant wilts.
An animal cell has no wall, so it bursts (haemolysis) in water and crenates in a concentrated solution.
